title: I Do Do

jokes.text: Previously on 30 Rock recap: Liz says she's going to marry 'Japheth,' live in 'Nineveh,' and be a 'Prostitute.'
jokes.setup: Previously on recap delivers dramatic romantic choices in the style of a soap opera cliffhanger
jokes.punchline: The destination and occupation escalate into increasingly Biblical absurdity, ending on 'Prostitute' as if it's a reasonable life plan
jokes.explanation: The escalating Biblical list (Japheth, Nineveh, Prostitute) is a compact absurdist joke delivered in recap format — the structure uses the 'rule of three' perfectly, with the third item being the comedic gut-punch. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: It's possible. Haven't you ever read Archie comics?
jokes.setup: Someone confronts Liz about being in love with two people simultaneously, treating it as a dramatic confession
jokes.punchline: Liz casually defends polyamorous feelings by citing Archie comics as a legitimate philosophical framework
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke. The Archie comics reference is completely unexpected yet instantly legible — everyone knows Betty vs. Veronica — and it perfectly encapsulates Liz's habit of using low-culture pop references to validate her emotional decisions. Character integration is exceptional: only Liz Lemon would cite a teen comic in a serious romantic confrontation. Maximum economy — the joke is six words.

jokes.text: You look amazing in that dress. / You look like a gay mortician in that suit.
jokes.setup: Jack compliments Nancy warmly and sincerely in a romantic moment
jokes.punchline: Nancy fires back with 'gay mortician' — a highly specific, devastating counter-compliment that deflates the sentiment
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'gay mortician' is what elevates this above a generic insult — it's precise, absurd, and yet somehow perfectly describes formal menswear gone wrong. The structural contrast (sincere compliment → brutal specific roast) is crisp. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Junior in-charge boy of the entire NBC page program.
jokes.setup: Jack delivers what should be an impressive job title promotion to Kenneth
jokes.punchline: The title 'Junior in-charge boy' is simultaneously grandiose and deeply demeaning — it sounds made up and infantilizing
jokes.explanation: The corporate title parody works because it sounds exactly like something NBC would actually call a job — the word 'boy' in there is the kicker, undermining what should be a dignified promotion. Solidly crafted but not exceptional.

jokes.text: My best friend in the whole world, comma, bald category.
jokes.setup: Kenneth expresses warm affection for his boss/mentor by calling him his best friend in the whole world
jokes.punchline: The qualifier 'comma, bald category' reveals Kenneth sorts his friendships by physical characteristic, implying many categorized best friends
jokes.explanation: An exceptional character joke. The 'comma, category' structure is uniquely Kenneth's — it reveals a bizarre internal taxonomy of friendships that is simultaneously sweet and deeply weird. Only Kenneth Parcell would categorize his best friends this way. The joke gets even richer on rewatch because you realize he must have an entire filing system of best friends. Very high character integration score.

jokes.text: I want to find long red hairs in my overcooked pot roast.
jokes.setup: Jack delivers a romantic speech to Nancy about the specific things he loves about being with her
jokes.punchline: Among tender romantic desires, he includes finding hair in badly cooked food — treating a domestic failure as a term of endearment
jokes.explanation: Clever subversion of the romantic speech formula — instead of idealized love, Jack's version includes specifically bad cooking and hair contamination. It characterizes both Jack (nostalgic for authenticity) and Nancy (not a great cook) simultaneously. The specificity of 'overcooked' and 'long red' elevates it above generic.

jokes.text: You're like that Mormon guy on HBO who was in that tornado movie. The one with the girl with the forehead who was married to that Jewish guy.
jokes.setup: Nancy tries to make a cultural reference to illustrate she can't share Jack with another woman
jokes.punchline: She can't remember any of the names and describes the show/movies through increasingly vague physical and demographic descriptors, ending in total chaos
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly specific character joke for Nancy — she's clearly referring to 'Big Love' and a Helen Hunt movie but describes them through a mom's imprecise pop-culture memory. 'The girl with the forehead' is hilarious. The joke satirizes how non-media-savvy people consume entertainment, and her punchline 'What? I'm a mom. Give me a break.' perfectly seals it. High character integration.

jokes.text: What? I'm a mom. Give me a break.
jokes.setup: Jack looks confused after Nancy's rambling, incomprehensible cultural reference
jokes.punchline: Nancy's self-defense is simply 'I'm a mom,' treating motherhood as a universally understood excuse for pop-culture illiteracy
jokes.explanation: Solid button to the preceding joke. Economy is perfect — three words do all the work. The implicit logic (moms don't know things, that's just how it is) is funny in its confident self-acceptance.

jokes.text: Maybe I'm old-fashioned, but when a girl dates a straight man who impersonates her on stage for mostly gay audiences, she has certain expectations. Fidelity, Paul. It's not just the name of a bank that sued me.
jokes.setup: Jenna confronts Paul about his infidelity — but the entire premise of their relationship (man impersonates girlfriend) is itself absurd
jokes.punchline: She frames the world's most non-traditional relationship as 'old-fashioned' and then adds that 'Fidelity' is not just a bank that sued her
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The joke operates on two levels simultaneously: the absurdity of Jenna calling herself 'old-fashioned' given her relationship, and the throwaway revelation that a bank named Fidelity has sued her (implying financial crimes). Only Jenna Maroney could deliver this with complete sincerity. The 'Fidelity' wordplay is elegant and the background detail (sued by a bank) is perfectly economical world-building.

jokes.text: That came out wrong. [Paul, after telling Jenna to choose between herself and herself]
jokes.setup: Paul tells Jenna she has to choose 'it's her or me' — but both options are Jenna
jokes.punchline: He immediately recognizes the logical impossibility mid-sentence and delivers the lamest possible correction
jokes.explanation: Clean absurdist button. The joke works because the entire Jenna/Paul relationship is built on this paradox and the show refuses to explain it — the understatement of 'that came out wrong' is the correct comedic choice.

jokes.text: Tickle each other like teletubbies. That's how I used to explain it to my kids when they walked in on us.
jokes.setup: Nancy interrupts Jack's businesslike statement about having an hour between weddings to do something
jokes.punchline: She finishes the sentence with 'tickle each other like teletubbies' and casually reveals this is how she described sex to her children who repeatedly walked in
jokes.explanation: The Teletubby euphemism is inspired — it's the perfect blend of innocent children's TV and deeply inappropriate adult activity. The added detail that kids walked in on them 'a lot' escalates the dark comedy. Character-specific for Nancy: the working-class mom using a kid's TV show to explain sex is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Two spider-mans fighting, and sometimes they make weird noises, but they're not hurting each other.
jokes.setup: Jack is delivering a serious speech about making bold decisions and pulling triggers
jokes.punchline: Nancy interrupts with another sex euphemism she told her kids, escalating from Teletubbies to Spider-Men
jokes.explanation: The escalation from Teletubbies to Spider-Man is perfectly judged. 'Sometimes they make weird noises, but they're not hurting each other' is a stunning encapsulation of how a parent desperately improvises sex explanations. This callback escalates the original joke and the new image is arguably funnier. High quotability — 'two spider-mans fighting' will stick in your head.

jokes.text: How often did they walk in on you? / A lot.
jokes.setup: Jack has been listening to Nancy describe multiple elaborate sex euphemisms she told her kids
jokes.punchline: His only question is the frequency, and her flat 'A lot' confirms the implication
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the sequence. Jack's deadpan curiosity and Nancy's matter-of-fact 'A lot' confirm a chaotic household without any further elaboration. The economy is excellent — 'A lot' does enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: D'oh, bother! Treble bother!
characters: Wesley Snipes (British character, not the actor)
jokes.setup: Wesley discovers he's left his fancy shoes behind — a problem that requires immediate solving
jokes.punchline: His exclamation is a mashup of Homer Simpson ('D'oh'), Pooh Bear ('bother'), and an invented intensifier ('Treble bother') — an absurdly British-American pop culture hybrid
jokes.explanation: Wesley's exclamation is a nicely constructed character-specific quirk — mixing D'oh with 'bother' and escalating to 'treble bother' characterizes him as an insufferable Anglophile-lite. Functional and specific but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Also Kevin in security has a picture of me.
jokes.setup: Wesley explains he can't return to his old office because he vowed on the Snipes name never to set foot there again
jokes.punchline: He adds, almost as an afterthought, that security has a photo of him — implying he's been barred/banned from the building for separate unspecified reasons
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock economy — a single throwaway line implies an entire backstory of professional misconduct. The casual delivery as a secondary reason makes it land harder than if it were the main point.

jokes.text: Fulfills my boyhood passion for train accidents.
jokes.setup: Liz notes that Wesley works in insurance specializing in the transportation industry
jokes.punchline: Wesley explains this career path fulfills his boyhood passion — for train accidents, not trains
jokes.explanation: The distinction between loving trains and loving train accidents is deceptively sharp — it takes a normal-sounding setup (boyhood passion for trains) and corrupts it with one word. Perfectly economical. The dark specificity of 'accidents' rather than 'trains' is the entire joke and it lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Farewell, my luscious plum.
jokes.setup: Wesley says goodbye to Liz before she goes to retrieve his shoes
jokes.punchline: He calls her a 'luscious plum' — a bizarrely fruit-based term of endearment that's simultaneously too intimate and deeply weird
jokes.explanation: A quick character gag — the affected, pompous endearment 'luscious plum' is very Wesley. Short, character-specific, gets a chuckle.

jokes.text: Also Kevin in security has a picture of me.
jokes.setup: Wesley explains he vowed never to return to the building after being fired.
jokes.punchline: He adds as an afterthought that security has a picture of him — implying he's been officially banned.
jokes.explanation: The casual addition of a deeply embarrassing fact (banned from the building) as a secondary reason not to return is good character economy. The nonchalance is the joke.

jokes.text: That's how I got out of doing foreplay with Angie.
jokes.setup: Tracy advises Kenneth to do a sloppy job to tank his promotion so they'll leave him alone
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals he uses the same 'sloppy job' strategy to avoid foreplay with his wife
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy non-sequitur confession — he pivots from professional advice to intimate domestic information without any sense that it's unusual. The specificity of 'foreplay with Angie' is very Tracy. High character integration.

jokes.text: And my taxes.
jokes.setup: Tracy advises the 'sloppy job' strategy works for avoiding foreplay
jokes.punchline: He casually appends 'and my taxes' — revealing a third context for deliberate incompetence
jokes.explanation: A perfect two-word escalation. The list — promotion avoidance, foreplay, taxes — is an absurd comedic trilogy delivered across two separate beats. 'And my taxes' is a clinic in economy: two words adding a legally alarming reveal.

jokes.text: If you've learned anything from me, it's how to do a bad job.
jokes.setup: Tracy is mentoring Kenneth about navigating his career
jokes.punchline: The lesson he imparts as a senior colleague/mentor is that the most important skill he's taught is doing a bad job
jokes.explanation: This lands because Tracy delivers it with complete sincerity — he genuinely believes incompetence is a teachable and valuable skill. It's a perfect inversion of the mentor-speech formula, and character-specific to Tracy who has built a career on erratic behavior.

jokes.text: Get it yourself, Chubbs. I'm on a coffee break.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Kenneth to 'honor me' and 'save yourself,' then asks him to get a sandwich — a classic authority move
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, just advised on how to do a bad job, immediately implements the lesson by refusing and calling Tracy 'Chubbs'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback payoff. Kenneth immediately applies the lesson he was just given, but the joke works on multiple levels: it's out of character for the eternally eager Kenneth, it pays off the immediately preceding setup, and 'Chubbs' is a perfectly chosen insult — affectionate yet cutting. Tracy's proud 'That's my boy' seals it. Excellent structural efficiency.

jokes.text: That's my boy. [Tracy's proud reaction to Kenneth calling him 'Chubbs']
jokes.setup: Kenneth refuses Tracy's sandwich request and insults him
jokes.punchline: Tracy responds with paternal pride, as if successfully teaching someone to disrespect him was his goal all along
jokes.explanation: Perfect button — three words completing the scene. Tracy's sincere pride in having taught Kenneth how to insult people flips the mentor dynamic beautifully.

jokes.text: Well, it's all true. I'm a native of Houston, and I love to cook healthy. And the female impersonator stuff.
jokes.setup: Jack says he's heard a lot about Paul (Jenna's boyfriend who impersonates Jenna on stage)
jokes.punchline: Paul confirms all of it — listing normal biographical facts (Houston, healthy cooking) alongside the extraordinary (female impersonation) with exactly equal weight
jokes.explanation: The deadpan normalization of female impersonation by placing it alongside Houston and healthy cooking is a clean structural joke. The matter-of-fact 'and the female impersonator stuff' as a casual afterthought is well-executed.

jokes.text: What if I could somehow combine them into one perfect woman, like a s'more you could take a shower with?
jokes.setup: Jack is advising Paul not to delude himself about loving two women — explaining the temptation is to try to combine them
jokes.punchline: His metaphor for the impossible ideal is 'a s'more you could take a shower with' — an image that is both evocative and completely insane
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The s'more metaphor is simultaneously sensual (warm, sweet, melty) and completely absurd (it would dissolve in the shower). It captures the impossible fantasy of combining two loves in a single image that is wildly specific and yet somehow perfectly evocative. This is 30 Rock at its peak — a joke that makes complete emotional sense while being completely bizarre. Jack Donaghy is the only character on television who would arrive at this metaphor. Highly quotable, rewatch-worthy.

jokes.text: Come on, Jessup. Get it together. No tears. [Avery talking to herself in mirror, Clamp down, Jessup! Be a winner.]
jokes.setup: Avery is clearly emotional in the bathroom but has to maintain her TV journalist composure
jokes.punchline: Her self-pep-talk is delivered in the tone of a sports coach or military commander, completely incongruous with the setting
jokes.explanation: A solid character-establishment joke. Avery's inability to emote without framing it as a competitive performance is well-characterized. The 'Be a winner' framing in a bathroom crying situation is the right comedic level for this character introduction.

jokes.text: Does the 'O' have it? 'O,' we do. Do you 'O'? 'O,' no? Let go. 'O.'
jokes.setup: Avery mentions her old CNBC show and Nancy misidentifies her from a commercial for 'Overshoppe.com'
jokes.punchline: Avery re-enacts the commercial jingle — a string of 'O' wordplay that becomes an absurd, endless loop of the vowel
jokes.explanation: A funny parody of aggressively branded early-2000s dot-com commercials. The jingle is absurdly committed to its single vowel gimmick. Works well as a character-deflating moment for Avery, showing she had humbler beginnings.

jokes.text: Ugh. That accent's idiotic.
jokes.setup: Avery has just finished re-enacting her own embarrassing commercial in her own former accent
jokes.punchline: She immediately distances herself from the accent she just demonstrated, critiquing it as idiotic
jokes.explanation: Quick button on the commercial bit. Avery's total lack of self-awareness about critiquing her own former accent (which she was JUST doing) is a clean character joke. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I can't drink this. [Avery reacts to cheap wedding champagne]
jokes.setup: Avery, clearly upset about seeing Jack with Nancy, is offered alcohol
jokes.punchline: After all the emotional turmoil, her visible distress is about the quality of the champagne — a comic deflection that also reveals her snobbery
jokes.explanation: Functional character gag establishing Avery as a snob. The beat relies on visual context (cheap wedding champagne vs. expensive tastes) which we infer. Competent but not especially original.

jokes.text: Oh, tuxedo slippers. Give me a break.
jokes.setup: Liz arrives at Wesley's office to retrieve his shoes, and discovers they are tuxedo slippers
jokes.punchline: Her exasperated reaction to the pretentious footwear — as if tuxedo slippers are the final straw in Wesley's insufferability
jokes.explanation: A quick reaction beat that works as character reinforcement for both Liz (exasperated, practical) and Wesley (pretentious). Modest but functional.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm a doorman... To the sky. I'm a pilot.
jokes.setup: A stranger asks Carol if he's a doorman (he's wearing a uniform at what appears to be an office building)
jokes.punchline: He plays along with 'doorman... to the sky' before clarifying he's a pilot — a self-aggrandizing yet dorky way to announce his profession
jokes.explanation: An excellent character introduction for Carol. 'Doorman to the sky' is both pompous and charming — it's the kind of thing a guy who is also sort of a dork would say to seem cool. Immediately establishes his voice.

jokes.text: Generally speaking, if there's a delay of more than 20 minutes, I might as well be driving a party bus.
jokes.setup: Carol explains how passengers got drunk during a weather delay
jokes.punchline: He characterizes his entire profession as equivalent to party bus driving when delays occur — a resigned, specific, and funny observation about air travel
jokes.explanation: A strong observational joke grounded in genuine air-travel experience. The 'party bus' framing is exactly specific enough to be funny while also being universally relatable.

jokes.text: People wear flip-flops to church. And the NBA tattoo situation is out of control.
jokes.setup: Carol says 'I don't know what's going on in this country' complaining about drunk passengers
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately chimes in with her own list of societal grievances — flip-flops at church and NBA tattoos — a random but very Liz curated list of personal outrage
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'NBA tattoo situation' is very funny — it's an oddly specific complaint that feels authentic to a certain kind of person. This exchange works as a meet-cute for Liz and Carol: they bond over shared curmudgeonliness.

jokes.text: A terrorist? / No. I wish. It's a drunk lady.
jokes.setup: Carol describes hearing a commotion in the cabin and going to investigate
jokes.punchline: Liz guesses 'terrorist' — and Carol's 'No. I wish' reveals that a terrorist would have been more professionally manageable than a drunk woman
jokes.explanation: Outstanding dark comedy. 'No. I wish.' is one of the episode's best lines — the implied logic (a terrorist follows rules, a drunk lady follows none) is sound, absurd, and deeply funny. The setup is perfectly structured: Liz's guess is reasonable given the setup, which makes the subversion more effective. Very quotable, high impact.

jokes.text: Sky law. It's when I put on the 'fasten seatbelt' sign, and no one's allowed to move till we've had ten minutes of silence. I made the whole thing up. But, you know, people are stupid, so they don't question it.
jokes.setup: Carol describes implementing 'sky law' to deal with the unruly drunk passenger
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals 'sky law' is entirely his own invention, sustained by passenger gullibility — and he's completely fine with this
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedy of authority abuse. The concept of 'sky law' — a completely made-up regulatory framework deployed by a single pilot — is a perfect absurdist invention. What makes it especially good is Carol's casual admission that he fabricated it combined with his zero remorse. 'People are stupid, so they don't question it' is the dark cherry on top. Establishes Carol as a lovably flawed authority figure.

jokes.text: She was bagging pretty hard on my TGS... Basically the greatest thing ever on television.
jokes.setup: Carol explains why he got into a confrontation with the drunk passenger
jokes.punchline: He was defending TGS (the fictional show within the show) from criticism and characterizes it as 'basically the greatest thing ever on television' — which is obviously absurd given what we've seen of the show
jokes.explanation: A nice meta-joke — the show within the show is being praised by a stranger on a plane as 'the greatest thing on television,' which is funny because the show within the show is notoriously mediocre. Also serves as a clever meet-cute accelerant.

jokes.text: There's the one fart doctor sketch where this fart doctor's trying to figure out who farted in the spelling bee, and he's like... 'He who spelt it, dealt it.' / I wrote that. I write all of the fart doctors.
jokes.setup: Carol excitedly recounts his favorite TGS sketch to impress Liz, not knowing she writes it
jokes.punchline: The sketch is absurdly lowbrow (fart doctor + spelling bee = 'he who spelt it, dealt it'), and Liz's proud ownership of it — 'I write all of the fart doctors' — deflates any prestige
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered joke. On one level it's a parody of terrible late-night sketch comedy; on another it's a perfect meet-cute beat (his enthusiasm about her embarrassing work makes her fall for him); and 'I write ALL of the fart doctors' is a brilliantly sad/proud line. The pun 'he who spelt it, dealt it' in a spelling bee context is genuinely clever wordplay buried inside an intentionally dumb sketch. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Would you like to go to a rich girl's wedding with me? / I don't know. Does that sound like more fun than me eating alone at the LaGuardia Chili's?
jokes.setup: Liz impulsively invites a stranger to a wedding
jokes.punchline: Carol weighs the invitation against his alternative: eating alone at an airport Chili's — suggesting this is a genuine deliberation and not obviously a better option
jokes.explanation: The LaGuardia Chili's is a perfect specific detail — it's the saddest possible dining alternative, both as an airport Chili's and as something done alone. That he treats this as a genuine comparison is beautifully character-establishing. Works wonderfully as a meet-cute punchline.

jokes.text: Good afternoon, and welcome... Not. / We begin our stupid tour of this once-great network outside studio 6H.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is giving a tour to Kabletown executives but has been advised to do a bad job
jokes.punchline: Kenneth begins the tour with 'welcome... Not' and calls it a 'stupid tour of this once-great network' — performing bad hosting while still being earnest about it
jokes.explanation: Kenneth implementing Tracy's advice is funny because his version of 'bad' is still structured and polite. 'Welcome... Not' is a dated 90s insult that sounds exactly like Kenneth's idea of rebellious. The phrase 'once-great network' is a nice bit of show self-awareness.

jokes.text: We begin our stupid tour of this once-great network...
jokes.setup: Kenneth is trying to give a deliberately bad tour.
jokes.punchline: He calls it a 'stupid tour' of this 'once-great network' — institutional self-deprecation that is still delivered with some residual reverence.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the Kenneth-trying-to-be-bad joke. The 'once-great' qualifier shows he can't help but be honest and a little mournful even in his sabotage attempt.

jokes.text: Let's meet up later and smoke some drug cigarettes.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is on his phone during the tour, pretending to be distracted and unprofessional
jokes.punchline: His attempt at sounding cool and delinquent is 'drug cigarettes' — a terminally square person's idea of what bad boys say
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. 'Drug cigarettes' is a masterpiece of Kenneth-voice — it's what someone who has never done drugs and doesn't know the vocabulary would call marijuana. The term is both hilariously innocent and perfectly logical from his perspective. Only Kenneth Parcell would say 'drug cigarettes.' Among the episode's best lines. Very high quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: You know what a great pilot would have done? Not hit the birds. That's what I do every day — not hit birds. Where's my ticket to the Grammys?
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably Jack) mentions Sully Sullenberger, the pilot who famously landed on the Hudson
jokes.punchline: Carol dismisses Sullenberger by pointing out that the actual skill is not hitting birds — something he does daily without recognition
jokes.explanation: An outstanding dark comedy bit. The logic is airtight: Sullenberger is celebrated for heroically managing a crisis he was partially responsible for (technically you're not supposed to hit birds), while every pilot who successfully avoids birds gets zero credit. 'Where's my ticket to the Grammys?' is brilliantly wrong (Grammys are for music) — Carol either misspoke or genuinely thinks the Grammys are the pinnacle of achievement. Either reading is funny. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: The usual ladies' room nonsense. Girl with boyfriend troubles. Someone forgot tampons. Everybody's bad at science and math.
jokes.setup: Jack asks what took Nancy so long in the bathroom — expecting a simple answer
jokes.punchline: Nancy casually summarizes the entire ladies' room social ecosystem, culminating in 'everybody's bad at science and math' as if this is a standard ladies' room complaint
jokes.explanation: The escalating list joke works perfectly — the first two items (boyfriend troubles, forgotten tampons) are stereotypically plausible ladies' room issues, which sets up the curveball of 'everybody's bad at science and math' as if that's what women discuss while fixing their makeup. It's a sharp satirical joke about gender stereotypes that nonetheless lands purely as comedy because of the list structure. Nancy's casual delivery is crucial.

jokes.text: Smug 40-year-old bridesmaid. What a treat for everyone.
jokes.setup: Liz is at the wedding as a bridesmaid and encounters Jack
jokes.punchline: Jack's description of Liz as a 'smug 40-year-old bridesmaid' is both accurate and devastating — and 'what a treat for everyone' is withering sarcasm
jokes.explanation: A clean Jack-to-Liz put-down. The specificity of '40-year-old bridesmaid' hits because it's culturally loaded (the 'always a bridesmaid' cliché), and 'what a treat for everyone' is perfectly arch. Well-crafted within the Jack/Liz dynamic.

jokes.text: You can't force your fate. You just have to let it wash over you, like a spray tan that won't take because your skin is too oily.
jokes.setup: Liz is dispensing romantic wisdom to Jack about fate and choice
jokes.punchline: She extends the metaphor into spray tan territory — but specifically a failed spray tan on oily skin — undercutting her own philosophical point with a very specific personal beauty problem
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon joke construction — she begins with genuine wisdom, then extends the metaphor into her own specific, unglamorous personal experience. The spray tan failing because of oily skin is such a specific, self-deprecating detail that it works beautifully as character comedy. Only Liz would undercut a philosophical point with a beauty product complaint.

jokes.text: It isn't made by those who don't do. It's made by those who do do, which is what made me the man I am. I do do. / Yeah. / Grow up, Lemon.
jokes.setup: Jack is making a serious speech about people who take action versus those who don't
jokes.punchline: His phrasing forces him to say 'do do' repeatedly with increasing solemnity, while Liz reacts like a middle schooler, and Jack has to tell her to grow up — which validates that she heard 'doodoo'
jokes.explanation: This is also the episode's title joke. The joke works on multiple levels: the wordplay (do do = doodoo), the character dynamic (Jack's pomposity vs. Liz's immaturity), and the fact that the episode is NAMED after this joke. Jack saying 'I do do' with complete gravitas while Liz can't contain herself is a perfect encapsulation of their relationship. 'Grow up, Lemon' as the button is ideal.

jokes.text: Kenneth, you're not going to Los Angeles. Oh. Because they're making me fire you. You're fired.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is told he's not going to Los Angeles, which seems like good news
jokes.punchline: The reason he's not going is that he's been fired — the relief is immediately inverted into disaster
jokes.explanation: A tight misdirection joke. The pause between 'You're not going to L.A.' and 'because they're making me fire you' is a classic beat that milks the false relief perfectly. Kenneth's 'Oh' in between is the ideal reactive beat. Well-constructed in very few words.

jokes.text: Well, I like how she's less hot than you.
jokes.setup: Nancy sincerely asks Jack to tell her what's special about Avery — a vulnerable emotional moment
jokes.punchline: Jack's first item is that Avery is 'less hot' than Nancy — an honest answer that is catastrophically wrong for the situation
jokes.explanation: Jack's brutal honesty is his character's defining trait, and starting a 'what I love about her' speech with 'she's less hot than you' is perfectly Jack — he genuinely means it as a compliment to both women and is completely unaware of how it lands. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Her laugh is like music. / Really mean music.
jokes.setup: Jack romantically describes Avery's laugh as being 'like music'
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies it as 'really mean music' — maintaining the metaphor while revealing it's not a compliment
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. The setup ('like music') is genuinely romantic, and 'really mean music' subverts it while maintaining the poetic structure. It also characterizes Avery — someone whose laugh is mean but appealing to Jack specifically. Economy is outstanding: four additional words completely flip the meaning.

jokes.text: She always wears high heels because, according to her, flat shoes are for quitters.
jokes.setup: Jack is describing Avery's specific qualities to Nancy
jokes.punchline: 'Flat shoes are for quitters' — Avery's actual stated philosophy on footwear, which reveals her as intensely competitive about everything including shoe choice
jokes.explanation: An excellent character-defining line for Avery. 'Flat shoes are for quitters' is the kind of line that writes an entire personality — it's aggressive, competitive, slightly insane, and somehow admirable. Very quotable. It makes you instantly want to know Avery better. High character integration for both Avery (defined) and Jack (who finds this attractive).

jokes.text: And by the way, when I blew your mind last night, I was giving it about 50%.
jokes.setup: Nancy is graciously stepping aside and telling Jack to be with Avery, which should be a tender farewell moment
jokes.punchline: As a parting shot, she reveals that the sex that 'blew his mind' was only half-effort — a competitive exit flex
jokes.explanation: Exceptional exit joke for Nancy. It's emotionally resonant (she's clearly hurt) while also being a completely badass flex. The '50%' detail makes it specific and thus more devastating. It characterizes Nancy as someone with tremendous self-possession even in defeat. One of the episode's strongest character moments doubled as a joke.

jokes.text: Unhand my fiancee! / No, no, he's just a groomsman. And a Somali pirate. Careful.
jokes.setup: Wesley makes a dramatic entrance to prevent Liz from leaving him
jokes.punchline: Liz clarifies to Carol that the man threatening him is 'just a groomsman. And a Somali pirate.' — delivered as a calm, practical warning
jokes.explanation: The casual addition of 'and a Somali pirate' to what should be a reassuring statement is perfectly absurdist. Liz treating this as ordinary biographical information is very 30 Rock. 'Careful' as the button is correctly underplayed.

jokes.text: You tried to end our engagement with a textual transmission. Your behavior as a fiancee has been as weak as American tea.
jokes.setup: Wesley confronts Liz about trying to break off their engagement
jokes.punchline: 'Textual transmission' for text message is absurdly formal, and 'weak as American tea' is a very British insult that implies the British standard for tea is the correct benchmark for fiancee behavior
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: 'textual transmission' is a wonderful pompous circumlocution for 'text,' and 'weak as American tea' is a perfectly specific cross-cultural insult. Wesley using British tea standards as a metric for romantic commitment is excellent character writing.

jokes.text: Your behavior as a fiancee has been as weak as American tea. There. I've said it.
jokes.setup: Wesley is mounting an argument for why Liz should stay with him.
jokes.punchline: 'As weak as American tea' — a British insult revealing his true national grievance — then 'There. I've said it.' as if this is a profound admission.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Wesley joke. 'As weak as American tea' is both a culturally specific British insult and an inadvertent self-exposure — he's been holding this grievance in. 'There. I've said it.' treats his national teatime complaint as a profound confession. Could only be Wesley. Very quotable.

jokes.text: His name is Carol. Like Carroll O'Connor from Nick at Nite. / Exactly, Cerie. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Liz rhapsodizes about meeting her fated man named Carol, a traditionally female name
jokes.punchline: Cerie's Carroll O'Connor reference (Archie Bunker) is completely random and slightly wrong (why Nick at Nite?), and Liz validates it as if it's exactly right
jokes.explanation: A quick double-character joke — Cerie's reference to Archie Bunker as a romantic ideal is an odd choice, and Liz's immediate 'Exactly, Cerie. Thank you.' is funny because she's so desperate for validation she'll take it from anyone, even this one.

jokes.text: And someday, when Carol sees my disgusting foot secret, he's gonna be okay with it. I can tell.
jokes.setup: Liz proclaims her faith in Carol and their future.
jokes.punchline: She's confident he'll accept her 'disgusting foot secret' — previously established as a mystery.
jokes.explanation: Maintains the running gag about Liz's mysterious foot condition. Works as character comedy and romantic optimism simultaneously — her idea of romantic faith is that he'll accept her foot situation.

jokes.text: And someday, when Carol sees my disgusting foot secret, he's gonna be okay with it. I can tell.
jokes.setup: Liz is giving a romantic speech about finding her soulmate
jokes.punchline: She inserts 'disgusting foot secret' into what should be a pure romantic moment — a specific, unelaborated horror that is funnier for being unexplained
jokes.explanation: The 'disgusting foot secret' is a master class in specificity and restraint — it's horrifying precisely because it's never explained. The contrast between this and the tender romantic speech around it is perfect. 'I can tell' as a sincere romantic qualifier makes it even funnier. This is great Liz Lemon character writing.

jokes.text: There's only one Wesley Snipes in this world. / You know there isn't.
jokes.setup: Wesley tries to make a grand, dramatic exit statement about his own uniqueness
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately and flatly points out that there is, in fact, a very famous Wesley Snipes — the actor — which undercuts his entire dramatic exit
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the Wesley Snipes name joke that runs throughout the series. Liz's flat, four-word refutation is perfectly timed and delivered. It's a callback to the entire season's running joke about his famous name, deployed at the most dramatically satisfying moment. Economy is nearly perfect — 'You know there isn't' does everything.

jokes.text: You walk briskly in a pilot's uniform, you can go pretty much anywhere. I've been upstairs in the White House while the Obamas were sleeping.
jokes.setup: Liz asks how Carol got past wedding security
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals that pilot uniform authority extends to the White House — including the residential quarters, while the first family slept
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The joke escalates perfectly: 'pilot uniform = access anywhere' is already funny, then 'I've been upstairs in the White House while the Obamas were sleeping' takes it to a genuinely alarming place. The specificity of 'while they were sleeping' is the key detail that makes it both sinister and absurd. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I'm sure you could get a cab on Houston. / Yeah, I'm gonna depart. On time. I'm a pilot.
jokes.setup: After Liz's speech, Carol realizes he overheard too much and is leaving awkwardly
jokes.punchline: He announces his departure using aviation language ('depart. On time.') and then clarifies 'I'm a pilot' — as if that explains the vocabulary
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Carol can't stop applying aviation language to normal life. Functional and character-consistent but not among the episode's strongest.

jokes.text: Ugh. Is there gay juice in the champagne?
jokes.setup: Avery, a tough, competitive newswoman, is expressing unexpected romantic feelings
jokes.punchline: She attributes her sentimental feelings to 'gay juice in the champagne' — a completely invented substance that she uses to deny genuine emotion
jokes.explanation: Excellent Avery character joke. 'Gay juice' is an absurd invention that makes perfect sense for this character — she's so unable to process emotional vulnerability that she needs a fictional pharmaceutical explanation. The fact that she says this to Jack, essentially complaining about her own feelings, is great. Very quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: See. I want you to teach our child how to say awesome stuff like that.
jokes.setup: Avery says something bizarre/aggressive ('gay juice in the champagne') in response to romantic feelings
jokes.punchline: Jack's response is not to correct her but to express genuine enthusiasm for her parenting their child to say things like that
jokes.explanation: Jack finding the 'gay juice' comment aspirational as a parenting goal is a perfect character beat — it shows exactly why Jack loves Avery. The joke works because his reaction validates her worst impulses.

jokes.text: Keeping it tight to stay camera-ready for breaking news.
jokes.setup: Avery is listing her concerns about the challenges of motherhood alongside career demands
jokes.punchline: She lists 'keeping it tight to stay camera-ready for breaking news' as a legitimate motherhood challenge on par with career and work-life balance
jokes.explanation: Character-specific joke for Avery — the vanity of TV journalism expressed as a genuine life concern. 'Camera-ready for breaking news' as a fitness goal is a sharp satirical observation about female news anchors' body pressure.

jokes.text: I mean, sure, Soledad O'Brien does it, but— / I wipe the floor with that bitch.
jokes.setup: Avery is wavering about whether she can handle motherhood and a career
jokes.punchline: She brings up Soledad O'Brien as a successful example — then immediately dismisses any self-doubt by aggressively asserting superiority over a colleague she's never actually competed with
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'I wipe the floor with that bitch' as a response to her own self-doubt — using competitive aggression to resolve an internal confidence crisis — is perfect Avery characterization. The joke also works as a proposal acceptance ('let's do this' follows immediately). The delivery must be instant and aggressive to work, and it's written that way. Highly quotable, high character integration, very funny. One of the better anchor-comparable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Love is weird and sometimes gross.
jokes.setup: A wedding officiant is delivering the traditional 'love is patient, love is kind' ceremony language
jokes.punchline: After 'love is patient,' he departs completely from scripture with 'love is weird and sometimes gross'
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical subversion of the wedding ceremony cliché. 'Weird and sometimes gross' works because it's honest, unexpected, and the kind of non-denominational officiant improv that is painfully real. Good structure — it follows the 'love is X' pattern faithfully before breaking.

jokes.text: To Grizz and Feyonce.
jokes.setup: A toast is made at the wedding reception
jokes.punchline: The bride's name is 'Feyonce' — a phonetic play on Beyoncé and 'fiancée' that only works as a name for a character in this universe
jokes.explanation: A wonderful background-character joke. 'Feyonce' is a triple pun (fiancée + Beyoncé + the Jay-Z connection of Grizz being her groom) that rewards attentive listeners. It's delivered casually, which makes it land harder. Grizz's girlfriend being named Feyonce is the perfect 30 Rock world-building detail.

jokes.text: On behalf of Grizz and Feyonce, I'd like to thank Jack Donaghy for letting us have this reception here after the other location couldn't support the weight of Grizz's extended family.
jokes.setup: A grateful thank-you speech is being given at the reception
jokes.punchline: The reason the original venue failed is that it structurally could not support the combined weight of Grizz's extended family — a devastating visual implied by a single sentence
jokes.explanation: A nicely underplayed dark joke delivered in the most inappropriate possible setting (a grateful toast). The structural failure of a venue due to family weight is committed to without apology. Grizz's size is already established, making this feel earned.

jokes.text: Naturally, I blew it. Now I'm alone in a dashiki. I wonder what that Somali pirate's deal is. I could live on a boat.
jokes.setup: Jenna is processing her romantic situation alone at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Her spiral from 'blew it' to 'alone in a dashiki' to immediate replacement romance with a Somali pirate happens in four sentences
jokes.explanation: This is a compact character monologue — Jenna's emotional processing is immediate and unserious. The pivot from heartbreak to 'I could live on a boat' while eyeing a pirate is pure Jenna narcissism. 'I'm alone in a dashiki' as a specific form of romantic tragedy is funny.

jokes.text: Yeah. Let's go lez. / No, I meant, like, a book club or something. Jeez.
jokes.setup: Liz and Jenna agree to support each other as a sisterhood alternative to men
jokes.punchline: Jenna interprets Liz's vague 'we've got each other' as a proposal to become romantically/sexually involved — and Liz has to clarify she meant a book club
jokes.explanation: Functional misdirection joke — Jenna's interpretation reveals her character (everything is sexual to Jenna) while creating a quick comedic beat. Not especially original but well-executed within the scene.

jokes.text: You have a lot of taped-up balls to come here dressed like that.
jokes.setup: Paul arrives at the wedding dressed as Jenna (in drag/female impersonation)
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'taped-up balls' is her version of 'balls' — acknowledging the physical reality of Paul's drag appearance while using it as an insult/compliment
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly specific wordplay joke. The expression 'a lot of balls' gets modified to 'taped-up balls' — acknowledging the literal physical fact of Paul's drag costume while using it idiomatically. It's a pun that is also character-specific: only Jenna would make this exact joke in this exact way. Original and economical.

jokes.text: I'm the man here, and you're gonna respect me. / Yes, shma'am.
jokes.setup: Paul, dressed as Jenna, asserts dominance in their relationship by declaring 'I'm the man here'
jokes.punchline: Jenna's submission is 'yes, shma'am' — a portmanteau of 'sir' and 'ma'am' appropriate for addressing someone who is presenting as a woman but claiming male authority
jokes.explanation: Exceptional wordplay. 'Shma'am' is an invented portmanteau that is linguistically elegant, plot-appropriate (Paul is dressed as a woman claiming male status), and instantly comprehensible. It's a neologism that makes immediate sense. The economy is perfect — one invented word does all the work. Among the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Lemon, you know that's a young boy's puberty dashiki.
jokes.setup: Liz is wearing a colorful dashiki to the wedding
jokes.punchline: Jack identifies it with the specific and absurd category of 'young boy's puberty dashiki' — implying this is a recognized garment type with a specific demographic
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully specific absurdist fashion commentary. The combination of 'young boy's' + 'puberty' + 'dashiki' creates a highly specific garment category that sounds exactly like something from a very niche catalog. Jack's complete confidence in identifying this is perfect. The specificity of 'puberty' as the type modifier is the joke.

jokes.text: Wrong, Jack. It's a warlord's concubine dashiki.
jokes.setup: Jack identifies Liz's dashiki as a 'young boy's puberty dashiki'
jokes.punchline: Liz corrects him with equal confidence: it is specifically a 'warlord's concubine dashiki' — an equally specific but completely different absurd category
jokes.explanation: The perfect callback and escalation to Jack's joke. The two-joke exchange works as a complete unit: Jack's categorization is absurd, but Liz's correction is MORE absurd and equally confident. 'Warlord's concubine dashiki' is a masterpiece of specificity — it implies an entire wardrobe taxonomy. The joke also works on the character level: Liz shopping from 'warlord's concubine' fashion lines is very funny. One of the episode's best exchanges.

jokes.text: I'm not surprised. Why should I be? / And I'm pregnant. / Also not shocking me. Reacting appropriately.
jokes.setup: Avery arrives and is informed of surprising developments (Jack's presence, her pregnancy)
jokes.punchline: She performs total composure by announcing her own emotional state as if narrating herself — 'reacting appropriately' as a self-directed stage direction
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Avery characterization. Her self-commentary ('Reacting appropriately') is the comedic peak — she's so committed to professional composure that she has to consciously direct her own emotional reactions like stage directions. Only Avery would say this. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Those dirtbags can wait on the runway a couple more hours. I hate people too.
jokes.setup: Liz points out that Carol has a flight — implying he should leave
jokes.punchline: He casually dismisses his passengers as 'dirtbags' who can wait on a runway while he pursues romance — a deeply unprofessional statement delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Good character reinforcement — Carol's contempt for his passengers (established earlier with 'people are stupid') is escalated here to actively stranding them. 'I hate people too' as a romantic bonding statement is a nice touch.

jokes.text: That was a joke. I have medicine for it.
jokes.setup: Carol mentions her 'disgusting foot secret' from the speech he overheard
jokes.punchline: Liz nervously clarifies it was a joke — then immediately validates that there is something with 'I have medicine for it'
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Liz's denial ('that was a joke') followed immediately by the admission ('I have medicine for it') is a classic comedy structure — the denial confirms the truth. The joke also characterizes Liz's self-sabotage instinct. Very well-executed.

jokes.text: As long as you're not Jewish. I'm totally kidding.
jokes.setup: Carol is agreeing to give their relationship a shot
jokes.punchline: He adds 'as long as you're not Jewish' — then immediately says he's kidding — but the speed of the denial doesn't fully erase the weirdness
jokes.explanation: A slightly uncomfortable joke that relies on the 'I'm kidding' escape hatch to defuse it. It establishes Carol as someone who says things he shouldn't, which is character work, but the joke itself is more edgy than crafted. Functions as a character wart.

jokes.text: And honestly, Carol, I am a very normal person.
jokes.setup: Liz assures Carol she's normal right before they're immediately interrupted by Jenna/Paul/Cher chaos
jokes.punchline: The reassurance is immediately undercut by the absurd scene that follows — the audience knows it's false
jokes.explanation: A setup for the visual chaos that follows — the joke is in the ironic juxtaposition of the claim with the evidence. Functional irony but not especially crafted on its own.

jokes.text: I can't believe I'm meeting 1 1/2 Jenna Maroneys right now.
jokes.setup: Carol meets Jenna and Paul (who is dressed as Jenna) simultaneously
jokes.punchline: '1 1/2 Jenna Maroneys' is the mathematically precise description of meeting one real Jenna and one Jenna impersonator
jokes.explanation: Very smart visual math joke. '1 1/2 Jenna Maroneys' is the exact right fraction — Paul is clearly less than a full Jenna but more than zero. The precision is what makes it funny. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody. I got fired today. You won't have Kenneth Ellen Parcell to kick around anymore, so I want to tell you people what I really think of you.
jokes.setup: Kenneth announces he was fired and is going to tell everyone what he really thinks — the setup for a drunken speech of grievances
jokes.punchline: The speech is set up as a big cathartic moment of Kenneth finally saying what he really feels
jokes.explanation: A well-structured setup for the extended Kenneth speech payoff. The 'You won't have X to kick around' Nixon reference is a nice cultural callback. Solid but the real payoff comes in the speech itself.

jokes.text: For four long years, I have listened to you all complain about your East coast media elite problems — your apartment renovations and your overpriced Star Wars memorabilia.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is delivering his big farewell grievance speech
jokes.punchline: His list of media elite complaints is: apartment renovations and overpriced Star Wars memorabilia — both extremely specific and accurate to the 30 Rock characters
jokes.explanation: Strong observational joke that works on two levels: it accurately parodies NYC media class concerns, and 'overpriced Star Wars memorabilia' is clearly a specific reference to someone in the writers' room or the cast's actual collecting habits. The list structure is correct — two items, with the second being more specific and funnier.

jokes.text: That doorman is hammered.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is delivering a passionate speech at the wedding reception
jokes.punchline: A wedding guest in the background assumes Kenneth is a drunk doorman — correctly identifying the energy while getting everything else wrong
jokes.explanation: A background reaction joke that works because it's simultaneously wrong (Kenneth isn't a doorman, isn't drunk) and weirdly right (he's acting exactly like a drunk doorman). Economy is perfect — four words.

jokes.text: I have watched you throw away better food than my family eats at Christmas.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is listing his grievances with the media elite he's worked for
jokes.punchline: His devastating class-contrast complaint: they throw away food that exceeds his family's best meal of the year
jokes.explanation: A genuine moment of pathos-comedy. The 'at Christmas' qualifier is the kicker — it's not just that his family eats poorly, it's that their special occasion meal is still worse than what these people discard. Kenneth's rural poverty is a recurring character element and this deploys it with real bite.

jokes.text: And I have loved it.
jokes.setup: Kenneth's speech has been listing grievances — poverty, being ignored, media elitism — building to what seems like a condemnation
jokes.punchline: The entire speech pivots to 'and I have loved it' — Kenneth genuinely loved all of it, including the abuse
jokes.explanation: The single best comedic moment in the episode. The entire speech has been structured as a grievance list — everything building to an expected outburst or condemnation. 'And I have loved it' as the pivot is the perfect Kenneth joke: his entire character (optimistic, unconditionally positive, incapable of genuine resentment) is expressed in five words that flip everything that came before. It's emotionally resonant AND funny. The structure is near-flawless — the longer the grievance list, the better the payoff. Character integration is as high as it gets: this is the Kenneth Parcell joke. Among the best jokes in the series.

jokes.text: So kiss my face!
jokes.setup: Kenneth has just delivered an unexpected declaration of love for everyone
jokes.punchline: His attempt at a defiant exit line is 'kiss my face' — a toothless, family-friendly version of 'kiss my ass' that perfectly captures Kenneth's inability to be truly profane
jokes.explanation: A masterful character joke. 'Kiss my face' is Kenneth's version of 'kiss my ass' — same rhythm, same defiant delivery, but completely neutered by his fundamental inability to be vulgar. The fact that he uses 'face' instead of 'ass' tells you everything about Kenneth Parcell. Delivered with full conviction after a touching speech, it's the perfect comedic capper. High quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: That was actually really sweet.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has just yelled 'kiss my face' as his defiant exit
jokes.punchline: Someone responds with 'that was actually really sweet' — the correct reading of what just happened, which is funnier than any more dramatic response
jokes.explanation: A functional button that correctly identifies the emotional register of Kenneth's speech. 'Actually really sweet' is the right deadpan reaction but isn't especially crafted on its own.

jokes.text: I'll see you all in heaven! / Have a wonderful summer!
jokes.setup: Kenneth is making his exit after his speech
jokes.punchline: He delivers two completely mismatched farewell statements — 'I'll see you all in heaven!' (eternal) followed immediately by 'Have a wonderful summer!' (yearbook-casual) — capturing Kenneth's tonal inconsistency
jokes.explanation: A perfect exit joke. The juxtaposition of the grandiose ('I'll see you all in heaven') with the mundane ('Have a wonderful summer!') is a rapid-fire tonal collision that perfectly encapsulates Kenneth — he oscillates between sincere religiosity and earnest small-talk without registering the tonal gap. 'Have a wonderful summer' is a yearbook sign-off, making it maximally incongruous after heavenly promises. Highly quotable.

tmdb_overview: Liz questions fate when she meets the man of her dreams, while Jack's love triangle between high school love, Nancy Donovan, and CNBC anchor, Avery Jessup, comes to a head. Meanwhile, Jenna's boyfriend is confronted with a similar dilemma when his desire for another woman threatens to ruin their relationship, and Kenneth, with the help of Tracy, tries to avoid a promotion that would land him in LA.
insight: Wedding chaos sustains 82-point score across 57 jokes in densest season finale.
